claim: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common and aggressive primary brain tumor among adults, with an average survival of less than 14 months despite aggressive surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy.
source: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common and aggressive primary brain tumor among adults, with an average survival of less than 14 months despite aggressive surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy (Stupp et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stupp et al., 2005, which is a reference to established literature on GBM survival rates.

claim: At most, 8% of GBM patients demonstrate long-term responses in ongoing PD-1 inhibitor trials.
source: At most, 8% of GBM patients demonstrate long-term responses in ongoing trials (Reardon et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Reardon et al., 2017, which provides clinical trial data on PD-1 inhibitor response rates.

claim: IDH-wildtype GBM tumors can be classified into three main categories: mesenchymal (MES), RTKI/proneural (PN), and RTKII/RTKIII/classical (CL).
source: Isocitrate Dehydrogenase (IDH)-wildtype GBM tumors can be classified based on genomic, transcriptomic, and DNA methylation data into three main categories, mesenchymal (MES), RTKI/proneural (PN), and RTKII/RTKIII/classical (CL) (Verhaak et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Verhaak et al., 2010, which describes the molecular classification of GBM.

claim: MES GBM accounts for 30–50% of primary tumors and is associated with particularly poor response to therapy.
source: MES GBM accounts for 30–50% of primary tumors and is associated with particularly poor response to therapy, while PN GBM is associated with a somewhat better prognosis.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about GBM subtypes and their clinical characteristics.

claim: Some reports have shown an enrichment of PD-L1LOW specimens in PN GBM and PD-L1HIGH specimens in MES GBM.
source: While some reports have shown an enrichment of PD-L1LOW specimens in PN GBM and PD-L1HIGH specimens in MES GBM (Berghoff et al., 2015), PD-L1 tumor expression has not been shown to directly predict clinical outcomes (Taube et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Berghoff et al., 2015 and Taube et al., 2014, which provide data on PD-L1 expression patterns.

claim: PD-L1 tumor expression has not been shown to directly predict clinical outcomes.
source: While some reports have shown an enrichment of PD-L1LOW specimens in PN GBM and PD-L1HIGH specimens in MES GBM (Berghoff et al., 2015), PD-L1 tumor expression has not been shown to directly predict clinical outcomes (Taube et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Taube et al., 2014, which discusses the limitations of PD-L1 as a predictive biomarker.

claim: GBM contain a highly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment with abundant tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) and low number of cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs).
source: In addition, GBM contain a highly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment with abundant tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), low number of cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) (Razavi et al., 2016; Nduom et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Razavi et al., 2016 and Nduom et al., 2015, which characterize the GBM immune microenvironment.

claim: TAM represents the majority of immune population in GBM (30%–50%).
source: TAM represents the majority of immune population in GBM (30%–50%), and high TAM density correlates with poor prognosis, and resistance to the therapy (Hambardzumyan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hambardzumyan et al., 2016, which provides data on TAM prevalence in GBM.

claim: High TAM density correlates with poor prognosis and resistance to therapy in GBM.
source: TAM represents the majority of immune population in GBM (30%–50%), and high TAM density correlates with poor prognosis, and resistance to the therapy (Hambardzumyan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hambardzumyan et al., 2016, which discusses the clinical significance of TAM density.

claim: GBM secrete immunosuppressive factors including transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1) and colony-stimulating factor-1 (CSF-1) polarizing monocytes toward an immunosuppressive 'M2-like' phenotype.
source: We (Lu-Emerson et al., 2013; Cui et al., 2018) and others (Thomas et al., 2012) recently demonstrated that GBM secrete immunosuppressive factors including transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1), and colony-stimulating factor-1 (CSF-1) polarizing monocytes toward an immunosuppressive 'M2-like' phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lu-Emerson et al., 2013, Cui et al., 2018, and Thomas et al., 2012, which provide experimental evidence for GBM-mediated macrophage polarization.

claim: An in silico analysis found that the M2-TAM gene signature indicated a greater association with the MES subtype (13%) compared to the non-MES subtypes: CL (6%) and PN (5%).
source: An in silico analysis of immune cell types in patient GBM biopsies found that the M2-TAM gene signature indicated a greater association with the MES subtype (13%) compared to the non-MES subtypes: CL (6%) and PN (5%) (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2017, which provides computational analysis of immune signatures in GBM subtypes.

claim: TAM-targeting agents like CSF-1R inhibitor have shown promise by reprogramming M2-TAMs toward an anti-tumorigenic 'M1' phenotype in murine glioma models.
source: TAM-targeting agents like CSF-1 receptor (CSF-1R) inhibitor have shown promise by reprogramming M2-TAMs toward an anti-tumorigenic 'M1' phenotype in murine glioma models, yet clinical trials on GBM patients showed poor response and patients acquired resistance by the tumor microenvironment (Pyonteck et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pyonteck et al., 2013, which provides preclinical data on CSF-1R inhibition.

claim: Clinical trials on GBM patients with CSF-1R inhibitors showed poor response and patients acquired resistance by the tumor microenvironment.
source: TAM-targeting agents like CSF-1 receptor (CSF-1R) inhibitor have shown promise by reprogramming M2-TAMs toward an anti-tumorigenic 'M1' phenotype in murine glioma models, yet clinical trials on GBM patients showed poor response and patients acquired resistance by the tumor microenvironment (Pyonteck et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pyonteck et al., 2013, which discusses clinical trial outcomes.

claim: A recent failed Phase III immunotherapy clinical trial (CheckMate-498: NCT02617589) emphasizes the need for better identification of patients that may benefit from immunotherapy.
source: A recent failed Phase III immunotherapy clinical trial (CheckMate-498: NCT02617589) (Hosea, 2019) emphasizes the need for better identification of patients that may benefit from immunotherapy.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hosea, 2019, which reports on the CheckMate-498 trial results.

claim: All patients in the study cohort were treated at NYU Langone Health between 6/1/2017 and 3/1/2019.
source: All patients were treated at NYU Langone Health between 6/1/2017 and 3/1/2019.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing the patient cohort.

claim: Patients received nivolumab 'off-label' for newly diagnosed or recurrent glioblastoma at 3 mg/kg intravenous injection every 14 days.
source: Patients received nivolumab 'off-label' for newly diagnosed or recurrent glioblastoma. Nivolumab was administered at 3 mg/kg intravenous injection every 14 days.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing the treatment protocol.

claim: Median duration of nivolumab therapy was 3.5 months (range 0.5 to 15 months).
source: Median duration of nivolumab therapy was 3.5 months (range 0.5 to 15 months).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Materials and methods section and represents clinical data from the patient cohort.

claim: PD-L1 staining was not predictive of response, showing both strong or no expression in both responders and non-responders across different GBM subtypes.
source: Our clinical data indicated that PD-L1 staining was not predictive of response, showing both strong or no expression in both responders and non-responders across different GBM subtypes (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 1B showing variable PD-L1 expression patterns.

claim: All tumors showed marked TAM infiltration by CD163, irrespective of molecular subtype.
source: Meanwhile, all tumors showed marked TAM infiltration by CD163, irrespective of molecular subtype (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 1B showing CD163+ TAM infiltration.

claim: GBM methylCIBERSORT analysis revealed prominent CD14 monocytic and neutrophilic DNA methylation and low CD8+ T-cell methylation signatures in MES patients.
source: GBM methylCIBERSORT analysis of a cohort of 435 glioma samples we previously profiled (Capper et al., 2018) further revealed prominent CD14 monocytic and neutrophilic DNA methylation and low CD8+ T-cell methylation signatures in MES patients, and low CD14 monocytic and neutrophilic DNA methylation and high CD8+ T-cell methylation in PN (RTK_I) patients (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA methylation deconvolution analysis presented in Figure 1C from a cohort of 435 glioma samples.

claim: PN (RTK_I) patients showed low CD14 monocytic and neutrophilic DNA methylation and high CD8+ T-cell methylation.
source: GBM methylCIBERSORT analysis of a cohort of 435 glioma samples we previously profiled (Capper et al., 2018) further revealed prominent CD14 monocytic and neutrophilic DNA methylation and low CD8+ T-cell methylation signatures in MES patients, and low CD14 monocytic and neutrophilic DNA methylation and high CD8+ T-cell methylation in PN (RTK_I) patients (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA methylation deconvolution analysis presented in Figure 1C.

claim: There was no significant difference between responders and non-responders in DNA methylation in immune cell signatures.
source: However, there was no significant difference between responders and non-responders in DNA methylation in these immune cell signatures (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of DNA methylation data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Clinicopathological methylation analysis revealed diverse immunosuppressive signatures in distinct GBM subtypes.
source: In addition, our clinicopathological methylation analysis also revealed diverse immunosuppressive signatures in distinct GBM subtypes, and some differences in epigenetic signatures between responders and non-responders (Figure 1D), but these were insufficient for predicting the response.
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA methylation analysis presented in Figure 1D showing differential methylation patterns.

claim: Current static biomarkers are poor predictors of anti-PD-1 immunotherapy response.
source: These data together confirm that current static biomarkers seem to be poor predictors of anti-PD-1 immunotherapy response, and a further analysis of the heterogeneity of the immunosuppressive GBM microenvironments might help identify niche-associated mechanisms for predicting and improving patient-specific responses to immunotherapy.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the clinical and experimental data showing lack of predictive value of PD-L1 and CD163 staining.

claim: The GBM-on-a-Chip system houses a 3D brain microvessel derived from human brain microvascular endothelial cells (hBMVECs).
source: In this organotypic system, we housed a 3D brain microvessel (Figure 2A–C, yellow) derived from human brain microvascular endothelial cells (hBMVECs), TAMs derived from human macrophages (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B), patient-derived and molecularly-distinct GBM cells (Figure 2A–C, red), and sorted allogeneic human CD8+ T-cells (Figure 2A–C, green) from primary peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) within a 3D brain-mimicking hyaluronan (HA)-rich Matrigel extracellular matrix (ECM) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Wang et al., 2019) (details see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the description of the GBM-on-a-Chip system and supported by images in Figure 2.

claim: TAMs in the GBM-on-a-Chip were derived from human macrophages.
source: In this organotypic system, we housed a 3D brain microvessel (Figure 2A–C, yellow) derived from human brain microvascular endothelial cells (hBMVECs), TAMs derived from human macrophages (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B), patient-derived and molecularly-distinct GBM cells (Figure 2A–C, red), and sorted allogeneic human CD8+ T-cells (Figure 2A–C, green) from primary peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) within a 3D brain-mimicking hyaluronan (HA)-rich Matrigel extracellular matrix (ECM) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Wang et al., 2019) (details see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the description of the GBM-on-a-Chip system and supported by supplementary figures.

claim: Biomimetic TAMs were nested within the 3D engineered HA-rich ECM tissue, making up 30% cell volume.
source: To reconstitute in vivo GBM tumor composition in vitro, biomimetic human TAMs were nested within the 3D engineered HA-rich ECM tissue (Figure 2F, blue), making up 30% cell volume (Hambardzumyan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to Hambardzumyan et al., 2016, which provides the rationale for the 30% TAM composition.

claim: TAMs were differentiated from U937 monocytes with Phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA) and treated with conditioned media from patient-derived adult GBM cells.
source: TAMs were differentiated from U937 monocytes with Phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA) and treated with conditioned media from patient-derived adult GBM cells of all three major molecular subtypes (Figure 2B; Shi et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to Shi et al., 2017, which describes the differentiation protocol.

claim: PN (GBML20) GBM exhibited significant increases both in the number and speed of allogeneic CD8+ T-cell infiltrate compared to the CL (GBML08) and MES (GBML91) GBM samples after 3 days' culture.
source: We demonstrated that PN (GBML20) GBM exhibited significant increases both in the number and speed of allogeneic CD8+ T-cell infiltrate compared to the CL (GBML08) and MES (GBML91) GBM samples after 3 days' culture (Figure 2G–I), which is consistent with our clinical observations (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 2G-I showing CD8+ T-cell infiltration and migration speed.

claim: The PN GBM demonstrated free, active motion of CD8+ T-cell while the degree of CD8+ T-cell motility was limited in the CL GBM and arrested in the MES GBM.
source: Moreover, we observed stark differences in T-cell migration trajectories, where the PN GBM demonstrated free, active motion of CD8+ T-cell while the degree of CD8+ T-cell motility was limited in the CL GBM and, arrested in the MES GBM (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by migration trajectory data presented in Figure 2H showing differential T-cell motility patterns.

claim: In the absence of TAM, increased number of allogeneic CD8+ T-cell extravasation (15 cell/mm2) was observed, suggesting that the presence of TAM inhibits CD8+ T-cell extravasation.
source: Interestingly, in the absence of TAM, increased number of allogeneic CD8+ T-cell extravasation (15 cell/mm2) was observed, suggesting that the presence of TAM inhibits CD8+ T-cell extravasation (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 comparing CD8+ T-cell extravasation with and without TAM.

claim: IL-2-activated allogeneic CD8+ T-cells showed higher apoptosis ratios of GBM cells compared to conditions without allogeneic CD8+ T-cells.
source: The cytotoxic activities of IL-2-activated allogeneic CD8+ T-cell on different subtypes of GBM cells were confirmed with a higher apoptosis ratios of GBM cells as compared to that of without allogeneic CD8+ T-cell in the niche (Figure 2J).
evidence: This claim is supported by apoptosis data presented in Figure 2J showing increased GBM cell death with CD8+ T-cells.

claim: Most of IL-2-activated allogeneic CD8+ T-cells expressed GZMB and CD69 but weak PFN after cultured in the GBM niches.
source: The on-chip staining showed that most of IL-2-activated allogeneic CD8+ T-cells expressed GZMB and CD69 but weak PFN after cultured in the GBM niches, while CD8+ T-cell in the MES GBM niche overall had lower expressions of these T-cell activation and cytotoxic function markers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting the immunosuppressive feature of the MES GBM niche.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 showing T-cell activation markers.

claim: CD8+ T-cells in the MES GBM niche had lower expressions of T-cell activation and cytotoxic function markers.
source: The on-chip staining showed that most of IL-2-activated allogeneic CD8+ T-cells expressed GZMB and CD69 but weak PFN after cultured in the GBM niches, while CD8+ T-cell in the MES GBM niche overall had lower expressions of these T-cell activation and cytotoxic function markers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting the immunosuppressive feature of the MES GBM niche.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and suggests an immunosuppressive mechanism.

claim: The ratio of activated CD154+CD8+ T-cells were markedly decreased in all GBM subtypes, more significantly in the MES GBM niche, compared to CD8+ T-cells cultured without the GBM niche.
source: Meanwhile, both immunostaining (Figure 3B) and qPCR analysis (Figure 3C) showed that the ratio of activated CD154+CD8+ T-cells were markedly decreased in all GBM subtypes, while more significantly in the MES GBM niche, when compared to CD8+ T-cells cultured without the GBM niche.
evidence: This claim is supported by both immunostaining and qPCR data presented in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: The immunosuppressive milieu hindered CTL activation and cytotoxic function at different levels of severity in molecularly distinct GBM subtypes.
source: It confirmed that the immunosuppressive milieu hindered CTL activation and cytotoxic function at different levels of severity in molecularly distinct GBM subtypes.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observed differences in CD154+ T-cell ratios and activation markers across GBM subtypes.

claim: The MES GBM tumor niche was characterized with highest expressions of PD-1 on CD8+ T-cell and PD-L1 on patient-derived GBM cell.
source: Particularly, the MES GBM tumor niche was characterized with highest expressions of PD-1 on CD8+ T-cell and PD-L1 on patient-derived GBM cell (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 3B showing PD-1 and PD-L1 expression levels.

claim: There was a significant number of immunosuppressive CD163+ M2-TAMs in the MES GBM compared to that in the PN and CL subtypes.
source: Both immunostaining (Figure 3D–E) and qPCR analysis (Figure 5C) results showed a significant number of immunosuppressive CD163+ M2-TAMs in the MES GBM compared to that in the PN and CL subtypes, which is consistent with our patient sample immunohistochemistry and methylCIBERSORT data (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by both immunostaining and qPCR data presented in Figure 3D-E and Figure 5C, and is consistent with patient data.

claim: CSF-1 was highly secreted in the MES GBM, compared to the PN and CL subtypes.
source: We demonstrated here that CSF-1 was highly secreted in the MES GBM, compared to the PN and CL subtypes using qPCR analysis (Figure 3C) and ELISA assay (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by both qPCR and ELISA data presented in Figure 3C and 3F showing CSF-1 levels.

claim: MES and CL GBMs likely had higher productions of anti-inflammatory cytokines TGF-β1 and IL-10, compared to the pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-α and IFN-γ.
source: Furthermore, our results showed that different GBM patient-derived cells showed distinct immunosuppressive cytokine milieus, and MES and CL GBMs likely had higher productions of anti-inflammatory cytokines TGF-β1 and IL-10, compared to the pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-α and IFN-γ (Figure 3G), driving TAM polarization toward a M2-like phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data presented in Figure 3G showing cytokine profiles across GBM subtypes.

claim: The IDH-mutant GBM (patient MGG152) showed similar cellular and cytokine conditions to the IDH-wildtype PN GBM in the on-chip study.
source: However, the IDH-mutant GBM (patient MGG152) showed similar cellular and cytokine conditions to the IDH-wildtype PN GBM in our on-chip study, which may be due to the poor survival capability of these IDH-mutant GBM cells when cultured in vitro (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 comparing IDH-mutant and PN GBM.

claim: Culturing tumor cells with the presence or absence of macrophages in the niche resulted in different epigenetic profiles.
source: We found that culturing tumor cells with the presence or absence of macrophages in the niche resulted in different epigenetic profiles and vice versa, the presence of GBM cell also altered the DNA methylation signatures of co-cultured macrophages (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole genome DNA methylation analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: The presence of GBM cells altered the DNA methylation signatures of co-cultured macrophages.
source: We found that culturing tumor cells with the presence or absence of macrophages in the niche resulted in different epigenetic profiles and vice versa, the presence of GBM cell also altered the DNA methylation signatures of co-cultured macrophages (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole genome DNA methylation analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: Rap1 signaling pathway was upregulated both in co-cultured GBM and macrophage cells, when compared to the GBM cells and macrophages in mono-cultures.
source: Rap1 signaling pathway, a known regulator of T-cell and antigen-presenting cells (Katagiri et al., 2002), was upregulated both in co-cultured GBM and macrophage cells, when compared to the GBM cells and macrophages in mono-cultures (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by KEGG pathway analysis presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and a citation to Katagiri et al., 2002.

claim: PD-L1 promoter methylation was slightly hypomethylated in mono- and co-cultured GBM cells.
source: Interestingly, PD-L1 promoter methylation was slightly hypomethylated in mono- and co-cultured GBM cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA methylation analysis of the PD-L1 promoter presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: BLZ945 suppressed the polarization of macrophages toward an immunosuppressive M2 phenotype in all three GBM subtypes with more significant CD163 marker suppression in the CL and MES GBM subtypes relative to the PN GBM.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Pyonteck et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2014), BLZ945 suppressed the polarization of macrophages toward an immunosuppressive M2 phenotype in all three GBM subtypes with more significant CD163 marker suppression in the CL and MES GBM subtypes relative to the PN GBM (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining and qPCR data presented in Figure 5B and 5C, and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: BLZ945 treatment alone caused no significant change in PD-L1 expression for both TAM and GBM cells.
source: However, BLZ945 treatment alone caused no significant change in PD-L1 expression for both TAM and GBM cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), implying that BLZ945 monotherapy cannot completely abolish the systemic immunosuppression in the GBM microenvironments.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 showing PD-L1 expression levels.

claim: CSF-1R blockade can significantly enhance allogeneic CD8+ T-cell extravasation across brain microvessels, compared to PD-1 blockade alone.
source: Our results indicated that CSF-1R blockade can significantly enhance allogeneic CD8+ T-cell extravasation across brain microvessels, compared to PD-1 blockade alone (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 5D showing CD8+ T-cell extravasation under different treatment conditions.

claim: Targeting TAM with BLZ945 alone did not significantly reverse the immunosuppression onto the cytotoxic CD8+ T-cell, compared to the untreated condition.
source: However, as demonstrated by profiling CD154 expression, targeting TAM with BLZ945 alone did not significantly reverse the immunosuppression onto the cytotoxic CD8+ T-cell, compared to the untreated condition (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by CD154 expression data presented in Figure 5E.

claim: PD-1 inhibition alone did not increase the extravasation of allogeneic CD8+ T-cell in GBM-on-a-Chip but did enhance CD8+ T-cell activation in the PN and MES GBMs.
source: In addition, PD-1 inhibition alone did not increase the extravasation of allogeneic CD8+ T-cell in GBM-on-a-Chip but did enhance CD8+ T-cell activation in the PN and MES GBMs.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data comparing PD-1 inhibition effects on T-cell extravasation and activation.

claim: PD-1 and CSF-1R dual blockade increased the extravasation of allogeneic CD8+ T-cell across brain microvessels.
source: PD-1 and CSF-1R dual blockade increased the extravasation of allogeneic CD8+ T-cell across brain microvessels (Figure 5D&E), reversed the immunosuppression onto CD8+ T-cell in terms of TNF-α and TGF-β1 production (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 2), and augmented CD8+ T-cell cytotoxic function with higher GBM tumor apoptosis shown by caspase-3/7 activation (Figure 5G–H, Figure 5—figure supplement 3) for each GBM subtype, specifically the MES GBM, compared to monotherapies.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 5D-H showing effects of dual blockade on T-cell extravasation and function.

claim: PD-1 and CSF-1R dual blockade reversed the immunosuppression onto CD8+ T-cell in terms of TNF-α and TGF-β1 production.
source: PD-1 and CSF-1R dual blockade increased the extravasation of allogeneic CD8+ T-cell across brain microvessels (Figure 5D&E), reversed the immunosuppression onto CD8+ T-cell in terms of TNF-α and TGF-β1 production (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 2), and augmented CD8+ T-cell cytotoxic function with higher GBM tumor apoptosis shown by caspase-3/7 activation (Figure 5G–H, Figure 5—figure supplement 3) for each GBM subtype, specifically the MES GBM, compared to monotherapies.
evidence: This claim is supported by cytokine data presented in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: PD-1 and CSF-1R dual blockade augmented CD8+ T-cell cytotoxic function with higher GBM tumor apoptosis for each GBM subtype, specifically the MES GBM, compared to monotherapies.
source: PD-1 and CSF-1R dual blockade increased the extravasation of allogeneic CD8+ T-cell across brain microvessels (Figure 5D&E), reversed the immunosuppression onto CD8+ T-cell in terms of TNF-α and TGF-β1 production (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 2), and augmented CD8+ T-cell cytotoxic function with higher GBM tumor apoptosis shown by caspase-3/7 activation (Figure 5G–H, Figure 5—figure supplement 3) for each GBM subtype, specifically the MES GBM, compared to monotherapies.
evidence: This claim is supported by apoptosis data presented in Figure 5G-H and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The presence of microglia in the GBM microenvironment could promote the PD-1 expression on allogeneic CD8+ T-cell.
source: Our results showed that the presence of microglia in the GBM microenvironment could promote the PD-1 expression on allogeneic CD8+ T-cell (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A), but there was no significant change observed in GBM cell apoptosis response to the PD-1 and CSF-1R dual blockade treatment compared to the macrophage only system (Figure 5—figure supplement 4B&C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 4A showing PD-1 expression with microglia.

claim: There was no significant change in GBM cell apoptosis response to the PD-1 and CSF-1R dual blockade treatment with microglia compared to the macrophage only system.
source: Our results showed that the presence of microglia in the GBM microenvironment could promote the PD-1 expression on allogeneic CD8+ T-cell (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A), but there was no significant change observed in GBM cell apoptosis response to the PD-1 and CSF-1R dual blockade treatment compared to the macrophage only system (Figure 5—figure supplement 4B&C).
evidence: This claim is supported by apoptosis data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 4B&C comparing conditions with and without microglia.

claim: Co-targeting M2-TAM could serve as a potential combinational therapy strategy for improving anti-PD-1 immunotherapy.
source: Altogether, our pre-clinical screening in the biomimetic GBM-on-a-Chip demonstrated that co-targeting M2-TAM could serve as a potential combinational therapy strategy for improving anti-PD-1 immunotherapy.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing improved outcomes with dual blockade therapy.

claim: GBM patients of transcriptionally defined subtypes have distinct epigenetic and immune signatures that may lead to different immunosuppressive mechanisms.
source: Our clinical and experimental data demonstrated that GBM patients of transcriptionally defined subtypes have distinct epigenetic and immune signatures that may lead to different immunosuppressive mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is based on the integrated analysis of clinical and experimental data showing subtype-specific differences.

claim: M2-like CD68+CD163+ TAMs dominated the immunosuppressive microenvironment in the MES GBM, by restricting the dynamics of CD8+ T-cell recruitment and activation.
source: Using our GBM-on-a-Chip model, we demonstrated that M2-like CD68+CD163+ TAMs dominated the immunosuppressive microenvironment in the MES GBM, by restricting the dynamics of CD8+ T-cell recruitment and activation, which can be effectively reversed with CSF-1R and PD-1 dual blockade therapy.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data showing TAM effects on T-cell behavior in the MES GBM subtype.

claim: Targeting PD-1 alone resulted in a modest effect on allogeneic CD8+ T-cell extravasation.
source: Similarly, targeting PD-1 alone resulted in a modest effect on allogeneic CD8+ T-cell extravasation.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data comparing PD-1 monotherapy effects.

claim: Microglia in the GBM microenvironment might have a similar immunosuppressive effect with the PBMC-derived macrophages on CD8+ T-cell PD-1 expression and functionality.
source: Our results indicated that microglia in the GBM microenvironment might have a similar immunosuppressive effect with the PBMC-derived macrophages on CD8+ T-cell PD-1 expression and functionality.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on experimental data comparing microglia and macrophage effects.

claim: BBB is uniformly disrupted in GBM which leads to leaky blood vessels.
source: However, it is well-established that BBB is uniformly disrupted in GBM which leads to leaky blood vessels (Sarkaria et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sarkaria et al., 2018, which describes BBB disruption in GBM.

claim: The aggressive TAM infiltration present in the perivascular, infiltrative and tumor bulk regions was concurrent with GBM tumor progression.
source: The aggressive TAM infiltration present in the perivascular, infiltrative and tumor bulk regions was concurrent with GBM tumor progression, indicating TAM-GBM tumor interactions contribute to the immunosuppressive GBM microenvironments and therapy resistance.
evidence: This claim is based on immunohistochemistry observations and infers a relationship between TAM infiltration and tumor progression.

claim: TAM-GBM tumor interactions contribute to the immunosuppressive GBM microenvironments and therapy resistance.
source: The aggressive TAM infiltration present in the perivascular, infiltrative and tumor bulk regions was concurrent with GBM tumor progression, indicating TAM-GBM tumor interactions contribute to the immunosuppressive GBM microenvironments and therapy resistance.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observed correlation between TAM infiltration and tumor progression.

claim: IDH-wildtype GBMs display a greater number of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and elevated PD-L1 expression compared to IDH-mutant GBMs.
source: IDH-wildtype GBMs have been reported to display a greater number of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and elevated PD-L1 expression compared to IDH-mutant GBMs (Berghoff et al., 2017), thus IDH mutational status may contribute differently to adaptive immune responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Berghoff et al., 2017, which reports on immune differences between IDH-wildtype and IDH-mutant GBMs.

claim: The interaction between TAM and GBM might regulate cytotoxic CD8+ T-cell activation via Rap1 signaling particularly in the CL GBM subtype.
source: Combined our DNA methylation results suggest that the interaction between TAM and GBM might regulate cytotoxic CD8+ T-cell activation via Rap1 signaling particularly in the CL GBM subtype.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on DNA methylation pathway analysis showing Rap1 signaling upregulation.

claim: PD-L1 expression was not epigenetically silenced in the absence of TAM.
source: Also, PD-L1 expression was not epigenetically silenced in the absence of TAM.
evidence: This claim is based on DNA methylation analysis of the PD-L1 promoter showing no significant hypermethylation.

claim: No significant changes in the deposition of HA, laminin, collagen IV and fibronectin were found in different GBM subtypes over 3 days.
